aspects.says: A subclass field with an inherited field's name hides it rather than overriding it: code compiled against the superclass keeps reading the superclass's field, so a varying value belongs behind an overridable method or a constructor argument.
basis: section:A Field Is Hidden, Not Overridden: the Declared Type Picks Which One Is Read

aspects.says: An override may widen the access of the method it overrides but never narrow it.
basis: section:An Override Can Widen Access but Not Narrow It, So a Subclass Can't Take a Method Away

aspects.says: In another package a subclass reaches a protected member only through references of its own type, while every class in the member's package reaches it freely.
basis: section:protected Reaches a Subclass in Another Package Only Through Its Own Type

aspects.says: A subclass can refuse an inherited operation only by throwing at run time, which breaks code written against the superclass.
basis: section:An Override Can Widen Access but Not Narrow It, So a Subclass Can't Take a Method Away
aspects.reason: a consequence the page states and shows in one sentence; substitutability is the subject of unit 8.1.3, which practises it

aspects.says: Superclass code reached through super still calls the subclass's overrides, so a subclass that overrides a method its superclass calls on itself depends on the superclass's undocumented implementation.
basis: section:Code Called Through super Still Calls Your Overrides, So a Subclass Depends on Its Superclass's Self-Calls

aspects.says: super.m() runs the direct superclass's version without dispatch; a cast of this to a superclass is still dispatched to the object's override, and super.super does not exist.
basis: section:super.m() Calls the Superclass's Version, and Nothing Reaches Past It
